- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.3) and forecast is significantly below recent highs, adjust upward by 1–2% to reflect bullish momentum.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) and forecast is above recent lows, adjust downward by 1–2% to reflect bearish sentiment.  
- When sentiment swings sharply upward after a dip, model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- If recent price history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days trending down), forecast should not anticipate further decline — add 1–3% upward bias to avoid underestimating rebound.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if last 5 days show strong upward momentum (e.g., >1% daily gain), model often underestimates continuation — add 2–5% to forecast tail.  
- If sentiment is neutral (0.1–0.2) and price is near 30-day moving average, forecast should be slightly below average to avoid overconfidence.  
- If forecast is consistently 3–5% below true outcome over 3–5 consecutive periods, apply upward bias of 3–5% for next forecast.  
- If sentiment is weak (≤ 0.1) and price is trending upward, model often underestimates momentum — add 1–3% to forecast to capture sentiment lag.
